body_markdown:
A new change to licensing rules is set to make it easier for people in England and Wales to prove their age when buying alcohol or entering age-restricted venues.


From Tuesday, 15 September 2026, licensed businesses will be able to accept approved digital identification as proof of age. The change means customers may be able to use their smartphones instead of carrying a physical driving licence, passport or other identity document.


The reform is being presented as a more convenient and potentially more privacy-friendly way to complete age checks. However, the system will initially be voluntary for both businesses and customers, meaning physical identification will continue to play an important role.


## What is changing?


Under the updated licensing arrangements, digital proof of age can be accepted when businesses need to establish whether a customer is legally old enough to purchase alcohol.


The change covers a range of licensed businesses, including pubs, restaurants, shops, music venues, concerts and festivals across England and Wales.


Rather than handing over a physical identity document, customers can use a compatible digital ID service on their phone. The technology is designed to allow a business to establish that someone meets the required age threshold without necessarily revealing additional personal details.


This could make the process quicker, particularly for people who do not want to carry valuable physical documents on a night out.


The Government has also indicated that digital verification could eventually have applications beyond alcohol sales. Tobacco products and vaping devices have been identified as areas where digital age verification could potentially be expanded.


## How could digital age checks work?


Digital age verification is expected to involve a combination of an identification app and technology used by the business.


A customer may first have to authenticate themselves through their phone. Depending on the service, this could involve entering a security code, using a PIN or completing a biometric check such as a facial scan.


Once the person's identity has been authenticated, the application can produce a temporary digital token, potentially in the form of a QR code.


The token is designed to be valid only for a short period. This helps reduce the risk of another person taking a screenshot or otherwise attempting to reuse somebody else's proof of age.


In some systems, a photograph may also be provided to a terminal so that staff can compare the customer with the person associated with the digital identity.


The exact experience could vary depending on which technology and provider a business chooses.


## You may not need to show your full identity


One of the arguments in favour of digital proof of age is that customers should not have to disclose more personal information than is necessary.


When showing a physical identity document, a customer could potentially reveal information such as their full name, address, photograph and date of birth.


A digital age-verification system can instead be designed to communicate a more limited piece of information, such as whether the individual has reached the required age.


That could provide a useful privacy benefit, particularly in situations where a customer only needs to demonstrate that they are legally old enough to buy a particular product.


However, the privacy protections will depend heavily on how individual digital identity systems are designed and operated. Customers should therefore pay attention to the information a particular service collects, stores and shares.


## Will every pub and shop accept digital ID?


No.


The new rules allow businesses to accept digital proof of age, but they do not require every licensed business to introduce the technology immediately.


That means customers should not assume that a digital ID will automatically be accepted everywhere.


Businesses may need compatible equipment or software, and some may choose to continue using traditional identification methods. Others could gradually introduce digital verification as the technology becomes more widely available.


The Government expects several providers to offer services rather than relying on a single application.


There is also an effort to make different systems interoperable. Ideally, customers would not need a separate application for every pub, shop or venue they visit.


## Physical ID is not disappearing


Despite the move towards digital verification, physical identification remains important.


The Government has said that physical ID will remain a valid way for customers to prove their age. Although the licensing changes create equivalence between digital and physical forms of proof, the expectation is that businesses will continue accepting traditional identification.


This is particularly important because not everyone owns a suitable smartphone, has reliable mobile access or wants to use a digital identity service.


Keeping physical options available also means customers are less likely to be excluded because of technical problems or personal preferences.


## Could the technology work without an internet connection?


Another important feature being considered is offline functionality.


Digital proof of age is expected to work offline in a similar way to contactless payment technology. If successfully implemented, this could be particularly useful in busy pubs, festivals and other venues where mobile connectivity may be unreliable.


The system would still need to provide businesses with confidence that the digital proof is genuine and has not been manipulated.


For customers, however, offline capability could make digital age verification much more practical in everyday situations.


## What does the change mean for businesses?


For hospitality and retail businesses, the introduction of digital proof of age could eventually reduce some of the friction associated with age checks.


Staff could potentially verify a customer's eligibility without examining a physical document in detail. It could also provide another option for customers who have forgotten to bring their driving licence or passport.


However, businesses will need to consider the practical costs involved.


The precise cost of implementing digital verification may vary depending on the provider and equipment required. Some systems may be capable of working with tablets or other devices that businesses already have.


Industry representatives have broadly welcomed the principle of digital proof of age while stressing the importance of making implementation affordable and straightforward.


## What happens next?


The introduction of digital proof of age is likely to be gradual rather than an overnight transformation.


The legal framework creates the opportunity for businesses to use digital identification, but widespread adoption will depend on technology providers, retailers, pubs, customers and regulators.


If the systems prove reliable and easy to use, digital age verification could eventually become a familiar part of buying age-restricted products.


There is also the possibility that the technology will be expanded to other products and services where proof of age is required.


For now, however, the most significant change is relatively simple: people in England and Wales may have another way to demonstrate that they are old enough to buy alcohol or access age-restricted venues.


## A shift towards digital age verification


The new rules represent another step towards using smartphones for everyday forms of identification.


For customers, the attraction is convenience. A digital ID could mean less need to carry physical documents, while temporary verification tokens could provide an additional layer of security.


For businesses, the technology could eventually make age checks faster and easier to manage.


There are still questions about adoption, privacy, costs and accessibility. Those issues will become clearer as more providers enter the market and more businesses begin using digital proof of age.


For the moment, the important point is that digital identification has gained a new legal role in age verification across England and Wales. Customers who prefer traditional identification can continue using physical documents, while those who choose digital verification will have another option when proving their age.


### Source


*The Independent* on 15 September 2026 concerning changes to licensing rules and the introduction of digital proof of age in England and Wales.


### Disclaimer


This article is provided for general informational purposes and should not be treated as legal advice. The availability, operation and acceptance of digital identification may vary between businesses and technology providers. Readers should check official Government guidance and the relevant business or service provider for the latest information before relying on digital ID as proof of age.
